guidance: A reference for cable drawings and orders, not an installation certificate. A Method names a whole channel of trunk, adapters, cords and transitions, and the parts of one method do not mix with another; check the vendor drawing and prove the channel with a polarity tester before relying on the link.
method: Each polarity method fixes one position-to-position mapping through a single 12-position trunk, and the page applies that mapping to a chosen duplex pair or transmit lane. Method A keeps every position in place, so position p reaches position p and a duplex pair arrives with transmit still on transmit; the channel needs one further transceiver-to-receiver flip, which TIA Method A supplies with a Type B cord at one end and a Type A cord at the other. Method B reverses the row, so position p reaches 13 - p: duplex pair n (fibres 2n-1 and 2n) lands on pair 7 - n with the two fibres swapped, which is the flip a parallel link needs, and the same cord type works at both ends. Method C crosses each adjacent pair, so position p reaches p+1 when p is odd and p-1 when p is even: the pair keeps its place while its fibres swap, which suits duplex transitions and is not recommended for parallel optics. A duplex pair at the near end is read as odd positions transmitting and even positions receiving, matching the usual LC cassette wiring, and an 8-fibre parallel application is read as transmit on positions 1 to 4 and receive on 9 to 12 with 5 to 8 unused, the Base-8 layout carried on a 12-position connector. The page covers one row of 12 positions: it does not model 16- or 24-position multi-row connectors, conversion harnesses, cassettes, MPO gender or polish, and it cannot tell what a particular cord or module does internally. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
